claim: Enhanced processing of attended stimuli waxes and wanes rhythmically during sustained attention, with periods of enhanced and relatively diminished visual processing alternating at 4 or 8 Hz.
source: Even during sustained attention, enhanced processing of attended stimuli waxes and wanes rhythmically, with periods of enhanced and relatively diminished visual processing (and subsequent target detection) alternating at 4 or 8 Hz in a sustained visual attention task.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work (Benedetto et al., 2020; Fiebelkorn and Kastner, 2019b) and is stated as an established finding in the abstract.

claim: Alternating attentional states occur alongside alternating dynamical states in which LIP, FEF, and mdPul exhibit different activity and functional connectivity at α, β, and γ frequencies.
source: These alternating attentional states occur alongside alternating dynamical states, in which lateral intraparietal cortex (LIP), the frontal eye field (FEF), and the mediodorsal pulvinar (mdPul) exhibit different activity and functional connectivity at α, β, and γ frequencies—rhythms associated with visual processing, working memory, and motor suppression.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations cited in the abstract and introduction, describing neural dynamics during attention tasks.

claim: The computational model of FEF and LIP, when driven by θ-rhythmic inputs simulating mdPul activity, reproduced the rhythmic dynamics and behavioral consequences of observed attentional states.
source: When driven by θ-rhythmic inputs simulating experimentally-observed mdPul activity, this model reproduced the rhythmic dynamics and behavioral consequences of observed attentional states, revealing that the frequencies and mechanisms of the observed rhythms allow for peak sensitivity in visual target detection while maintaining functional flexibility.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results presented in the manuscript, including simulations and analyses.

claim: Measuring the success of target detection as a function of the interval between presentation of a spatially predictive cue and a target reveals an oscillation in hit rates with 8 Hz periodicity at the cued location and 4 Hz periodicity at an uncued location.
source: measuring the success of target detection as a function of the interval between presentation of a spatially predictive cue and a target reveals an oscillation in hit rates with 8 Hz periodicity at the cued location and 4 Hz periodicity at an uncued location (Fiebelkorn et al., 2018; Fiebelkorn et al., 2013; Landau and Fries, 2012; Song et al., 2014; VanRullen et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies measuring behavioral performance in attention tasks.

claim: θ-rhythmic changes in behavioral performance are associated with θ phase-dependent dynamical states that alternate at 4 Hz and are characterized by distinct neural dynamics and patterns of functional connectivity between FEF and LIP.
source: Recordings from the frontal eye field (FEF) and lateral intraparietal area (LIP) in monkeys have revealed that θ-rhythmic changes in behavioral performance are associated with θ phase-dependent dynamical states, which alternate at 4 Hz and are characterized by distinct neural dynamics and distinct patterns of functional connectivity between these areas (Fiebelkorn et al., 2018; Fiebelkorn et al., 2019c).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental recordings from monkey electrophysiology studies.

claim: The mediodorsal pulvinar (mdPul) specifically coordinates cortical activity during the good θ phase but not during the poor θ phase.
source: with the mediodorsal pulvinar (mdPul)—a higher order thalamic nucleus associated with cognitive functions including attention (Halassa and Kastner, 2017; Fiebelkorn and Kastner, 2019a; Kastner et al., 2020; Saalmann and Kastner, 2011) and interconnected with the cortical nodes of the attention network (including LIP and FEF) in monkeys (Gutierrez et al., 2000; Romanski et al., 1997; Selemon and Goldman-Rakic, 1988)—specifically coordinating cortical activity during the θ phase associated with enhanced perceptual sensitivity (the 'good θ phase'), but not during the θ phase associated with relatively diminished perceptual sensitivity (the 'poor θ phase'; Fiebelkorn et al., 2019c).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies of thalamo-cortical interactions during attention tasks.

claim: The model replicated behavioral results, revealing how an 8 Hz behavioral oscillation at the cued location can arise from a 4 Hz alternation of dynamical states, in dependence on the strength of functional connectivity from LIP to FEF.
source: The model also replicated behavioral results, unexpectedly revealing how an 8 Hz behavioral oscillation (at the cued location) can arise from a 4 Hz alternation of dynamical states, in dependence on the strength of functional connectivity from LIP to FEF.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results showing the relationship between connectivity strength and behavioral oscillation frequency.

claim: Altering the timescale of the oscillatory dynamics in FEF or LIP resulted in decreased task performance.
source: We found that altering the timescale of the oscillatory dynamics in FEF or LIP resulted in decreased task performance, providing evidence for the functional significance of these rhythmic dynamics.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational experiments varying model parameters and measuring task performance.

claim: The model was constructed from biologically detailed neurons and is consistent with the known anatomy, physiology, and function of frontal and parietal circuits.
source: The model was constructed from biologically detailed neurons and is consistent with the known anatomy, physiology, and function of frontal and parietal circuits.
evidence: This claim is supported by the detailed description of the model construction in the Methods section and references to prior experimental work.

claim: The model was built on previous cortical models that reproduced experimentally observed network dynamics in the contexts of working memory and cholinergic neuromodulation.
source: Since small models with single-compartment neurons can be difficult to parametrize using electrophysiological measurements, we built on previous cortical models that reproduced experimentally observed network dynamics in other cognitive and physiological contexts—specifically, in the contexts of working memory and cholinergic neuromodulation (Kramer et al., 2008; Lee and Whittington, 2013; Gelastopoulos et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior computational modeling work that informed the current model.

claim: θ-rhythmic input from mdPul to cortex, subsequent to a spatially informative cue, can produce alternating dynamical regimes that explain periodicity in behavioral outcomes.
source: Our model shows how θ-rhythmic input from mdPul to cortex, subsequent to a spatially informative cue, can produce alternating dynamical regimes that, in turn, explain periodicity in behavioral outcomes (i.e. hit rates).
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results demonstrating the relationship between mdPul input and behavioral periodicity.

claim: The frequencies of observed rhythms maximize interactions between FEF and LIP and the sensitivity of target detection.
source: It shows that the frequencies of observed rhythms maximize these interactions and the sensitivity of target detection, suggesting that these rhythms, rather than being epiphenomena, are key to the function of attention in the brain.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational experiments showing that altering rhythm frequencies decreases task performance.

claim: LIP→FEF functional connectivity may contribute to the experimentally observed shift in hit rate periodicity from 4 Hz for the uncued object to 8 Hz for the cued object.
source: It suggests that LIP→FEF functional connectivity (operationalized as the maximal synaptic conductance) may contribute to the experimentally observed shift in hit rate periodicity from 4 Hz (for the uncued object, and reflecting the frequency of mdPul input) to 8 Hz (for the cued object).
evidence: This claim is based on the computational model's behavior showing how connectivity strength affects behavioral oscillation frequency.

claim: The LIP module combined two previous laminar models of working memory and attention.
source: The LIP module (Figure 3A) combined two previous laminar models of working memory and attention (Kramer et al., 2008; Lee and Whittington, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior computational models that were integrated into the current model.

claim: The second inspiration for the LIP module was a model of the effects of cholinergic modulation on the potentiation of γ power in the superficial layers of sensory cortex.
source: The second inspiration for the LIP module was a model of the effects of (attentional) cholinergic modulation on the potentiation of γ power in the superficial layers of sensory cortex (Lee and Whittington, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior computational work on cholinergic modulation.

claim: In the cholinergic modulation model, β rhythms delivered to deep layers activate SOM interneurons, which suppress granular layer FS cells, resulting in disinhibition of granular layer RS cells and a γ rhythm.
source: In this model, the excitation-inhibition balance in the granular layers is such that FS cells dominate RS cells, largely damping RS cell responses to excitatory input. In the presence of cholinergic modulation, β rhythms delivered to deep layers activate SOM interneurons, which in turn produce slowly decaying inhibition that suppresses granular layer FS cells. This results in disinhibition of granular layer RS cells, changing the excitation-inhibition balance sufficiently that RS cells drive FS cells to produce a γ rhythm.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior computational work on cholinergic modulation and describes the mechanism of γ rhythm generation.

claim: When disinhibition was combined with increased excitatory input to the granular layer, a γ rhythm resulted, which then propagated to the superficial layer.
source: When this disinhibition was combined with increased excitatory input to the granular layer, a γ rhythm resulted, which then propagated to the superficial layer.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results describing the mechanism of γ rhythm generation.

claim: FEF beta input to the deep layers of LIP created the potentiated γ in the superficial layers of LIP during the good θ phase.
source: Thus, as in the previous model (Lee and Whittington, 2013), FEF beta input to the deep layers of LIP created the potentiated γ in the superficial layers of LIP during the good θ phase (Figure 3B and C, E; also see Robustness and Flexibility of the LIP Module).
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results shown in Figure 3 and comparison to prior work.

claim: The FEF visuomotor module consisted of RS cells reciprocally inhibited by SOM cells.
source: The FEF visuomotor module consisted of RS cells reciprocally inhibited by SOM cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the model design illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: During the poor θ phase, the excitation-inhibition balance between SOM and RS cells in the FEF visuomotor module was such that the SOM cells silenced the RS cells.
source: During the poor θ phase, the excitation-inhibition (E-I) balance between SOM and RS cells was such that the SOM cells (activated by tonic excitation) silenced the RS cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results describing the dynamics of the FEF visuomotor module.

claim: During the good θ phase, RS cells in the FEF visuomotor module, stimulated by mdPul, fired and took control of SOM cell activity.
source: During the good θ phase, RS cells, stimulated by mdPul, fired and took control of SOM cell activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results describing the dynamics of the FEF visuomotor module.

claim: The FEF visual module determined the full model's response to target presentation by detecting the presence of a simulated target.
source: The FEF visual module—consisting of RS, FS, VIP, and SOM cells (Figures 1C and 5A)—determined the full model's response to target presentation, by detecting the presence of a simulated target.
evidence: This claim is supported by the model design and results shown in Figures 1C and 5A.

claim: The heart of the target detection circuit is the VIP–SOM interaction.
source: The heart of the target detection circuit is the VIP–SOM interaction: both of these cells receive enhanced visual input upon target presentation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the model design and analysis of the FEF visual module.

claim: VIP and SOM cells are known to mutually inhibit each other.
source: VIP and SOM cells are known to mutually inhibit each other (Tremblay et al., 2016), but while VIP have only local connections to SOM cells, SOM cells have global connections to VIP cells (Karnani et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies of VIP and SOM cell connectivity.

claim: VIP cells have only local connections to SOM cells, while SOM cells have global connections to VIP cells.
source: VIP and SOM cells are known to mutually inhibit each other (Tremblay et al., 2016), but while VIP have only local connections to SOM cells, SOM cells have global connections to VIP cells (Karnani et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies of VIP and SOM cell connectivity.

claim: VIP interneurons exhibit large responses to relatively small inputs.
source: The physiology of VIP interneurons—which exhibit large responses to relatively small inputs (Lee et al., 2010; Wall et al., 2016)—also played an important role in the model dynamics.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies of VIP interneuron physiology.

claim: When no target was present on screen, SOM cells were active, and SOM inhibition silenced VIP and RS cells in the FEF visual module.
source: When no target was present on screen, all SOM, RS and VIP cells in the module received input from LIP. The sizes of the inputs were such that SOM cells were active, and SOM inhibition silenced VIP and RS cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results describing the dynamics of the FEF visual module.

claim: When a target appeared, VIP cells in the stimulated cluster fired, temporarily silencing SOM cells and disinhibiting RS cells.
source: When a target appeared, a smaller γ input (coming from early visual areas, possibly via LIP) further excited the SOM, RS, and VIP cells of one cluster. Within this cluster, SOM cells, which were already highly active and exhibited a shallower f-I curve than the VIP cells (Appendix 1—figure 1; Wall et al., 2016; Millman et al., 2020), did not change their spiking pattern. The VIP cells in this cluster therefore received the same amount of inhibition, but a higher amount of excitation, which, due to their steeper f-I curve (Appendix 1—figure 1; Wall et al., 2016; Millman et al., 2020), caused them to fire. VIP firing then temporarily silenced SOM cells, disinhibiting RS cells and enabling them to fire.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results and citations to experimental data on VIP and SOM cell physiology.

claim: The interaction of VIP and SOM cells amplified a small difference in excitation between two visual regions, resulting in a large RS cell response to even a small increase in excitation.
source: Though such increased excitability of RS cells could be obtained though many different mechanisms, the interaction of VIP and SOM cells amplified a small difference in excitation between two visual regions, resulting in a large RS cell response to even a small increase in excitation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results and analysis of the FEF visual module.

claim: The VIP and SOM cell circuit in the visual module played an important role in the detection of near-threshold visual stimuli.
source: We hypothesize that these mechanisms play an important role in detecting near-threshold visual stimuli, such as the low contrast target of the task we are modeling.
evidence: This claim is based on the computational modeling results and represents a hypothesis about the functional role of the VIP-SOM circuit.

claim: The output of FEF visual and visuomotor RS cells was transmitted to a set of RS cells in the visuomotor module called decision cells, whose spiking activity was interpreted as initiating action in response to target detection.
source: The output of FEF visual and visuomotor RS cells was transmitted to a set of RS cells in the visuomotor module that we refer to as decision cells, whose spiking activity we interpreted as initiating action in response to target detection.
evidence: This claim is supported by the model design and interpretation of decision cell activity.

claim: Input from FEF visuomotor RS cells set the threshold for decision cell spiking, determining how likely they were to respond to input from FEF visual cells during target presentation.
source: Input from (non-decision-related) FEF visuomotor RS cells set the threshold for decision cell spiking, determining how likely they were to respond to (simultaneous) input from FEF visual cells during target presentation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the model design and analysis of decision cell behavior.

claim: The model's response to the target depended on its timing relative to the ongoing θ cycle.
source: The model's response to the target depended on its timing relative to the ongoing θ cycle (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results shown in Figure 6.

claim: The number of FEF decision cell spikes following target appearance was higher on average when the target appeared during the good θ phase compared to when it appeared during the poor θ phase.
source: More precisely, the number of FEF decision cell spikes following target appearance was higher on average when the target appeared (i.e. when target input began) during the good θ phase (or at the transition from poor to good θ phase) compared to when it appeared during the poor θ phase (or at the transition from good to poor θ phase; Figure 6C (i)).
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results shown in Figure 6C(i).

claim: Model hit rates varied with the cue-target interval and exhibited an 8 Hz θ rhythm, in agreement with behavioral data.
source: In agreement with behavioral data, model hit rates varied with the cue-target interval; somewhat surprisingly, they also agreed with behavioral results in exhibiting an 8 Hz θ rhythm (Figure 6C (iii) & (iv)).
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results shown in Figure 6C and comparison to experimental behavioral data.

claim: Increasing LIP→FEF connectivity increased both hit rates and false alarm rates.
source: Increasing LIP→FEF connectivity increased both hit rates (Figure 7A (i)) and false alarm rates (Figure 7A (ii)).
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Intermediate values of LIP→FEF connectivity resulted in the highest levels of task performance.
source: Computing the D' sensitivity index, which combines both hit and false alarm rates, revealed that intermediate values of LIP→FEF connectivity resulted in the highest levels of task performance (i.e. both high hit rates and low false alarm rates, Figure 7A (iii)).
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results shown in Figure 7A(iii).

claim: For sufficiently high values of the conductance of LIP→FEF chemical synapses, the temporal profile of hit rates exhibited a dominant 8 Hz component.
source: For sufficiently high values of the conductance of LIP→FEF chemical synapses, the temporal profile of hit rates exhibited a dominant 8 Hz component (Figure 7B), while for small values of the LIP→FEF conductance, the hit rates exhibited robust 4, 8, and 12 Hz periodicity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results shown in Figure 7B.

claim: 8 Hz rhythms in hit rate resulted from the addition of another, smaller peak in hit rate at the beginning of the poor θ phase.
source: Varying LIP→FEF conductance revealed that, while a hit rate peak at the beginning of the good θ phase (at 0 degrees) was common across 4 and 8 Hz hit rate rhythms, 8 Hz rhythms resulted from the addition of another, smaller peak in hit rate at the beginning of the poor θ phase (Figure 7B (i) & (ii)).
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The deployment of attention towards a cued object moderately increases the strength of LIP→FEF connectivity in neural populations representing that object, resulting in both an increase in performance and a change in the rhythmicity of behavior.
source: Our model is consistent with the hypothesis that the deployment of attention towards a cued object moderately increases the strength of LIP→FEF connectivity in neural populations representing that object, resulting in both an increase in performance (as reflected by an increase in D') and a change in the rhythmicity of behavior.
evidence: This claim is based on the computational modeling results and represents a hypothesis about the neural mechanisms underlying attentional modulation.

claim: The activation of FEF visual module SOM cells at a γ timescale provides a blanket of inhibition that prevents VIP cells from spiking outside of target presentation and reduces false alarms in the network during the good θ phase.
source: A key point is that the activation of FEF visual module SOM cells at a γ timescale, that is, faster than their β time constant of inhibition, provides a blanket of inhibition that prevents VIP cells from spiking outside of target presentation and reduces false alarms in the network during the good θ phase.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results and analysis of the mechanisms underlying task performance.

claim: Top-down signals from FEF function to increase the gain of LIP superficial layer spiking by disinhibiting the LIP granular layers.
source: In our model of the cued location, top-down signals from FEF function to increase the gain of LIP superficial layer spiking by disinhibiting the LIP granular layers.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results describing the mechanism of FEF-LIP interactions.

claim: Attentional modulation can be interpreted as the gain modulation of bottom-up input based on its expected reliability.
source: While our conception of attention is broader in general, we note that, in this case, attentional modulation can be interpreted as the gain modulation of bottom-up input based on its expected reliability.
evidence: This claim is based on the computational modeling results and represents an interpretation of the model's behavior in the context of predictive processing theories.

claim: The frequency of FEF and LIP oscillations in the model has consequences for task performance, and the values typically reported in experiments produce peak levels of sensitivity in the model attention network.
source: The frequency of FEF and LIP oscillations in our model has consequences for task performance, and the values typically reported in experiments in fact produce peak levels of sensitivity in our model attention network.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results showing that altering rhythm frequencies decreases task performance.

claim: The temporal dynamics of network activity provide periodic windows of enhanced sensitivity that enable precise monitoring of a given region of the visual field with acceptable temporal coverage, while also minimizing energetic cost and allowing monitoring to be interleaved with other computational imperatives.
source: The second is to provide periodic windows of enhanced sensitivity, that enable precise monitoring of a given region of the visual field with acceptable temporal 'coverage', while also minimizing energetic cost and allowing monitoring to be interleaved with other computational imperatives, including monitoring of other regions and motor planning and execution.
evidence: This claim is based on the computational modeling results and represents a hypothesis about the functional significance of rhythmic dynamics.

claim: The 8 Hz hit rates in the model did not come from the division of a 4 Hz rhythm into multiple possible target locations, but were a consequence of the increased LIP→FEF connection strength for the cued object.
source: In other words, the 8 Hz hit rates in our model did not come from the division of a 4 Hz rhythm into multiple possible target locations, as previously suggested for similar data (Landau and Fries, 2012), but were a consequence of the increased LIP→FEF connection strength for the cued object.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results and represents an alternative explanation to a prior hypothesis.

claim: The appearance of a cue on the screen might enhance LIP→FEF visual cell functional connectivity, leading to both increased perceptual sensitivity especially during the poor θ phase and an 8 Hz dominant frequency in the hit rate spectrum.
source: Our model thus suggests that the appearance of a cue on the screen might enhance LIP→FEF visual cell functional connectivity, leading to both increased perceptual sensitivity especially during the poor θ phase and an 8 Hz dominant frequency in the hit rate spectrum.
evidence: This claim is based on the computational modeling results and represents a hypothesis about the neural mechanisms underlying cue-related changes in behavior.

claim: Very strong LIP→FEF connectivity led to high false alarm rates, and such excessive connectivity may be linked to hallucinations or other pathologies in visual perception.
source: In our results, very strong LIP→FEF connectivity led to high false alarm rates, and such excessive connectivity may be linked to hallucinations (as in the detection of a target in the absence of a visual stimulus) or other pathologies in visual perception.
evidence: This claim is based on the computational modeling results and represents a speculation about the potential clinical relevance of the model.

claim: The θ rhythm may be a solution to the necessity of attending to multiple objects 'at once', allowing the focus of attention to switch between objects θ-rhythmically.
source: One possibility is that the θ rhythm is a solution to the necessity of attending to multiple objects 'at once', allowing the focus of attention to switch between objects θ-rhythmically.
evidence: This claim represents a hypothesis about the functional role of the θ rhythm in attention.

claim: The good and poor θ phases may result from an alternation between more and less specific hypotheses about the visual location of target appearance.
source: Alternatively, the good and poor θ phases may result from an alternation between more and less specific hypotheses about the visual location of target appearance.
evidence: This claim represents an alternative hypothesis about the functional role of the θ rhythm in attention.

claim: The break in attentional focus allowed by the poor θ phase would allow attention and behavior to adapt quickly to changes in visual stimuli and their perceived salience.
source: In either account, even when attention is deployed at a single location, the break in attentional focus allowed by the poor θ phase would allow attention and behavior to adapt quickly to changes in visual stimuli and their perceived salience.
evidence: This claim represents a hypothesis about the functional role of the poor θ phase in attention.

claim: The failure of a target to appear during the good θ phase may be seen as reducing confidence in the hypothesis that the target will appear at the cued location.
source: The failure of a target to appear during the good θ phase may be seen as reducing confidence in the hypothesis that the target will appear at the cued location.
evidence: This claim represents a speculation about the cognitive mechanisms underlying the alternation between good and poor θ phases.

claim: The poor θ phase could enable the planning and execution of motor actions.
source: Finally, it has been hypothesized that the poor θ phase could enable the planning and execution of motor actions (Fiebelkorn and Kastner, 2019b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior hypothesis about the functional role of the poor θ phase.

claim: The θ rhythm may be a mechanism that interleaves periodic assessment of multiple hypotheses about target appearance with motor execution.
source: The θ rhythm may be a mechanism that interleaves periodic assessment of multiple hypotheses about target appearance with motor execution, with movements occurring at the transitions between good and poor θ phases, each of which represents the sampling of evidence for one particular hypothesis.
evidence: This claim represents a hypothesis about the functional role of the θ rhythm in coordinating sensory and motor processes.

claim: All cell types were modeled as Hodgkin-Huxley point neurons, with spiking currents tailored with cell type-specific parameters.
source: All cell types were modeled as Hodgkin-Huxley point neurons, with spiking (i.e. leak, sodium, and potassium) currents tailored with cell type-specific parameters (see Tables 1–5 in Methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by the detailed description of the model in the Methods section.

claim: Vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) interneurons were modeled with a potassium D-current, and produced inhibition with a similar decay time to SOM cells, but spiked in response to much lower levels of excitation.
source: Finally, vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) interneurons were modeled with a potassium D-current, and produced inhibition with a similar decay time to SOM cells, but spiked in response to much lower levels of excitation (Appendix 1—figure 1), in accordance with experimental data (Tremblay et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by the model design and a citation to experimental data on VIP interneuron properties.

claim: VIP inhibition exclusively targets SOM interneurons in the model.
source: VIP inhibition exclusively targets SOM interneurons in our model (see Methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by the model design described in the Methods section.

claim: All neurons in the model received tonic excitation at cell-type-specific levels, encapsulating the effects of cell-type-specific resting membrane potentials and/or background inputs.
source: All neurons in the model received tonic excitation at cell-type-specific levels, encapsulating the effects of cell-type-specific resting membrane potentials and/or background inputs (that do not vary with θ phase) from other brain regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the model design described in the Methods section.

claim: mdPul input consisted of 12 Hz input nested in a 4 Hz θ rhythm, with the second pulse of 12 Hz input twice as large as the first.
source: This drive consisted of 12 Hz input nested in a 4 Hz θ rhythm; we assumed the θ rhythm would be sinusoidal or sawtooth-shaped, and that mdPul input would occur during the first half of the θ cycle (as seems to be the case experimentally; Fiebelkorn et al., 2018), so the second pulse of 12 Hz input was twice as large as the first.
evidence: This claim is supported by the model design and a citation to experimental observations.
